S. flava var. ornata 'black veins' Bulloch Co, GA clone D, pics taken 12/11/19. One of the original F2 clones that gave rise to the majority of black veined flavas in cultivation today. Interestingly, this is one of the few flava clones in the collection that still has a trap in perfect condition on it! Black veined flavas are famous for being able to produce fall traps, which is unusual for flavas in general. There are other flava clones that do produce traps throughout the winter (ie. S. flava var. rugelii from the extinct Defuniak Springs, FL site) but it's very rare.


clone D has a well defined red throat under optimal conditions. This isn't optimal conditions, but it's still pretty decent:

S. flava var. ornata black veins clone D Bulloch Co, GA has produced very late fall traps AGAIN! No idea why this clone seems to consistently bust out these pitchers! It's pretty neat because this is the only flava in the collection that has traps that look decent throughout the winter! Pics taken 12/11/20:







Clone D and one other original black veined flava clone producing late fall traps. This trait is potentially very valuable for those trying to breed plants with traps that last throughout the winter:

Yeah, that is interesting.

Normal degree of phyllodia production from the clones that send up these fall pitchers? Is there a second production of phyllodia after these fall pitchers?
posts.body_text:
Yeah, that is interesting.
Normal degree of phyllodia production from the clones that send up these fall pitchers? Is there a second production of phyllodia after these fall pitchers?

posts.body_html: Never even thought about that KE, thanks for asking!  I peeped out all the plants, and they produce their normal spring traps, followed by one or two phyllodia in the summer/fall.  The clones that are producing late fall traps also have that normal set of 1-2 phyllodia which are also produced in the summer/fall!  There is no other phyllodia produced after that last fall pitcher or two, just straight to dormancy.

posts.body_html:
The next time your black veined flava doesn't look black, don't panic because check this out! Here's S. flava var. ornata black veins clone D Bulloch Co, GA, one of the original black veined clones! this plant is one of the first plants in the collection to produce traps this year, and it's inexplicably early! Almost everything else is still pretty much dormant, we haven't finished trimming everything yet!

Notice the pitchers barely look black at all! It's been mostly cold and rainy this whole time, so not enough light or heat to get the traps looking like they normally do. The first spring traps are sometimes not as veined either, but that depends mostly on the environment. Pics taken 3/18/24:
